'Here it is,' Reena said, sliding a folder across the table. 'Twelve risks, twelve backup plans.'

'Even the one where the hall floods?' Kishore asked.

'Even that. Page nine.'

'And the demo? The main script for the demo?'

Reena looked at the folder. 'I'll do it tonight.'

'Reena, the client comes at ten tomorrow.'

'I know. I spent all week on the backups.'

The next day, after the client left, Kishore spoke quietly. 'The demo froze at slide four. We had no script for the normal path.'

'We had a plan for a flood, though,' Reena said, and rubbed both eyes. 'Nobody was ever going to ask about that.'

qa.q: How many backup plans did Reena write?
qa.a: Reena wrote twelve backup plans, one for each risk.

qa.q: How was Reena feeling when looking at the folder?
qa.a: Reena felt anxious and caught out, realising the main script was still not ready.

qa.q: What could Reena have done instead of covering all twelve risks?
qa.a: Reena could have chosen the two or three likely, costly risks for backup plans and spent most of the week preparing the main demo.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel about the frozen demo?
qa.a: Kishore may feel frustrated and worried, having asked about the main script the day before.

grounding: Shows a project lead writing backups for many unlikely risks and running out of time to prepare the main path.

subtype: Approach: plans for so many scenarios that the main plan is neglected [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Keerthana, and last year I led the move of our NGO's records to a new online system. I was determined nothing would catch us off guard.
So I wrote backup plans. What if the internet fails. What if the vendor shuts down. What if a volunteer deletes a file. What if there's a flood in the office. What if the software has a virus. Twelve risks, each with a two-page plan. My colleague Charu said, "Most of these won't happen." I said, better safe.
It took me three weeks. I felt very prepared.
What I hadn't done was the actual work. I hadn't cleaned the old data, trained the six volunteers, or tested the import even once.
On migration day, half the records came in with broken dates. Nobody knew how to fix them. None of my twelve plans covered it, because it wasn't a disaster. It was just the main job, not done.

qa.q: How many risks did Keerthana write plans for?
qa.a: Twelve risks, each with a two-page plan.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel after three weeks of writing backup plans?
qa.a: Keerthana felt very prepared and confident, which made the failure on migration day more of a shock.

qa.q: What would you change first in Keerthana's approach?
qa.a: Spend most of the time on the main path, cleaning data, training volunteers and a test import, and write backups only for the two or three most likely risks.

qa.q: How might Charu see migration day?
qa.a: Charu may feel frustrated and a little vindicated, having warned that most of the risks wouldn't happen.

grounding: It shows a project lead writing backup plans for twelve mostly unlikely risks and running out of time to prepare the main path, which then falters.

passage:
Supervisor's note, project review, 18 October
Mehak joined as project lead for the clinic booking system in August. She is careful and hardworking. Today's review showed what that can cost.
Her risk file is impressive: fourteen contingency plans, from server failure to a monsoon flooding the data centre to a vendor going bankrupt. Each has a flowchart. Baljeet, the developer on her team, told me she had spent most of September on them.
But the main path is behind. The appointment screen has not been tested with real clinic staff. The training guide is half written. Go-live is in eleven days.
When I asked about the testing, she looked stricken and said, "I thought if I covered every risk, the rest would be fine."
We agreed on a plan: freeze the contingency work, keep only the top three risks, and spend next week on testing and the training guide. I will check in on Friday.

qa.q: How many contingency plans are in Mehak's risk file?
How did Mehak feel when asked about the testing?
qa.a: She looked stricken, showing she was shocked and worried that the main work had been left behind.

qa.q: Which approach would have suited Mehak better from the start?
qa.a: Plan for the few likely and costly risks, then put most effort into testing and training on the main path.

qa.q: How might the clinic staff be affected if go-live happened as things stand?
qa.a: They might get a booking screen that was never tested with them and no finished training guide, which could make their work harder.

grounding: It shows a project lead writing backup plans for many unlikely risks and running out of time for the main path, which falls behind.
